title: From Income to Tax
subtitle: Tax law hierarchy, filing records and a reproducible 2026 Form 1040 income-tax computation
prerequisites: L1.S2 household cash flow and net worth
L6.S1 tax liability, deductions and compliance
L8.S2 the difference between earnings and cash receipts
objectives: Classify wage, business, interest, dividend, gain and excluded receipts under source rules
Distinguish gross pay, W-2 Box 1 wages, adjusted gross income and taxable income
Build an auditable 2026 federal income-tax waterfall including payments and refunds
Trace W-2, 1099-INT, 1099-DIV, 1099-B and Schedule 1 into a return
Compare a deduction, a refundable credit and a nonrefundable credit
Identify simplifications and missing schedules before estimating a real return

sections.title: What the tax system actually measures
body: Income tax starts from a legal definition of income rather than the cash that happens to land in a bank account. A salary deposit is commonly net of withholding and payroll taxes, but the income-tax return begins with taxable wages shown on Form W-2, Box 1. Borrowed money generally creates both cash and an obligation to repay, not taxable earnings. A transfer between one's own accounts is not new income. A gift, inheritance, insurance benefit, or canceled debt may have different rules; classification is determined by law and facts rather than by how a budgeting app labels the transaction.

The US federal income tax is legislated in the Internal Revenue Code, interpreted through regulations, administrative guidance and court decisions. A taxpayer should distinguish binding statutory rules from a marketing claim or an online chart. IRS publications and instructions are practical primary administrative guides, although the statute and regulations control when there is a conflict. Federal income tax is only one layer: payroll taxes, state income taxes, local property taxes, sales taxes and employer costs use different bases.

An income statement prepared for an employer, a lender and the IRS can display different numbers without contradiction. Gross compensation might be $90,000, taxable wages $84,000 after permitted pre-tax payroll reductions, annual direct deposits $65,000 after withholding and other deductions, and adjusted gross income a still different amount once investment receipts and allowed adjustments are added. Comparing tax liabilities using deposit totals would systematically misstate the return.
worked: Gross employer compensation: hypothetical $90,000.
If eligible salary deferrals excluded from W-2 Box 1 are $6,000, Box 1 wages may be $84,000.
A $65,000 net cash deposit is neither the taxable income figure nor the tax owed.
Reconcile the paystub, W-2, bank deposit and benefits documents before starting calculations.
practice: Why is a $5,000 personal loan deposit not generally $5,000 of taxable wages?
The loan produces cash paired with a repayment obligation; it is not compensation or realized enrichment. Cancellation of the debt can create different tax consequences.
A banking app shows $12,000 transferred from savings to checking as 'income.' What happens on a tax return?
The internal transfer normally creates no new taxable income. Confirm account ownership and source documents rather than importing the app category directly.

sections.title: Build a source-document map before calculating
body: Think of the return as a controlled information system. The employee W-2 reports wages and withheld federal income tax; 1099-INT reports interest; 1099-DIV distinguishes total ordinary dividends from the qualified subset; 1099-B lists securities dispositions and often reported basis; Schedule C reports business revenue less allowable business expenses; Schedule 1 gathers additional income and adjustments. Individual cases may need Schedules 2 and 3, credits and specialty forms. A reconciliation table should state payer, identifying form, tax year, dollar amount, classification, and whether the number is gross or net.

Do not add a qualified dividend amount on top of the total ordinary dividends when Form 1099-DIV shows that qualified dividends are already included in Box 1a. Likewise a broker's Form 1099-B gross proceeds are not income in full: capital gain is realized amount minus adjusted basis. A stock sale for $12,000 with $10,000 adjusted basis creates a $2,000 gain, not $12,000 of salary. Incorrect basis reported by a broker may require Form 8949 adjustments with supporting acquisition records.

Completeness matters more than the number of forms mailed. Taxable interest or side-gig receipts can require reporting even when no 1099 arrives. Keep a year-labeled folder with statements, purchase confirmations, dividend reclassification notices, basis adjustments, and estimated-payment confirmations. Do not place personal identifying numbers in the training app; the laboratory is deliberately anonymous and hypothetical.
worked: W-2 Box 1 wages $85,000; federal withholding Box 2 $13,000.
1099-INT taxable interest $1,000.
1099-DIV Box 1a dividends $1,500, of which Box 1b qualified dividends $1,500: include $1,500 in total income once.
1099-B: net long-term gain $4,000 after basis verification; total income $91,500.
practice: Why does adding both 1099-DIV Box 1a and Box 1b double-count income?
Box 1b is the subset of Box 1a eligible for special rate treatment, not a second independent dividend payment.
What evidence supports a Form 8949 basis correction?
Prior confirmations, transfer statements, reinvestment history, corporate-action records and brokerage basis data with acquisition dates form an audit trail.

sections.title: Timing, character and realization
body: Many individuals use cash-method reporting: taxable income is commonly recognized when actually or constructively received, subject to specific rules. A pay period spanning December and January is typically governed by when the pay becomes available, not simply the days worked. In contrast, a portfolio's unrealized appreciation is usually not taxable solely because its market value rises. A sale or another taxable disposition normally makes a gain or loss realized. Tax law also includes special recognition regimes, such as some distributions and mark-to-market elections, so 'nothing taxed until sold' is not a universal law.

Character is as important as timing. Wage and taxable bank interest commonly use ordinary-income rates. A qualifying dividend or a net long-term capital gain may use preferential rates. Self-employment profit may also generate self-employment tax independent of regular income tax. Municipal bond interest can be excluded from regular federal income tax in qualifying circumstances but may require state-specific treatment and reporting. The return should identify each type before combining totals.

Construct a transaction journal with date acquired, date disposed, proceeds, eligible sale costs, adjusted basis, holding period, and tax character. For multiple lots of one fund, independent verification is essential: a dividend reinvestment can create a new basis lot even though no cash was withdrawn. This discipline is the bridge from Module 8 portfolio accounting to Module 11 taxes.
worked: Security purchased for $7,000; year-end value $8,200: unrealized gain $1,200, generally no sale-triggered federal capital gain.
Sell next year for $8,500 with $50 selling expense: amount realized $8,450.
Adjusted basis $7,000 gives realized gain $1,450.
A stock held for one year or less generally produces short-term gain; more than one year generally produces long-term gain.
practice: When can a paper gain become a tax item?
Usually when a sale or other taxable disposition is recognized; timing exceptions exist under particular tax rules, so identify the asset and event.
Why does a tax worksheet need a holding-period field?
The holding period helps determine whether gain is short-term or long-term and therefore whether ordinary or preferential federal rates may apply.

sections.title: Adjusted gross income is not taxable income
body: The basic federal income-tax waterfall is total income, minus qualifying adjustments to income, equals adjusted gross income (AGI); then subtract allowable deductions to reach taxable income. AGI is a gating figure for many credits and phaseouts. Not every expense paid out of a paycheck is an allowable above-the-line adjustment. A contribution to an employer's traditional 401(k) generally reduces W-2 Box 1 wages before the return; deducting it again as an AGI adjustment would be double counting.

Schedule 1 Part II includes specific allowed adjustments such as certain deductible IRA contributions and HSA contributions where eligibility rules are met; the law imposes caps, timing conditions and phaseouts. A traditional 401(k) salary deferral is different from a Roth 401(k) contribution and different from buying an ETF inside a taxable account. The account label alone does not prove a deduction. A taxpayer must check employment coverage, filing status, income limits and plan documents.

An AGI adjustment can have an indirect value beyond its straightforward marginal rate. Lower AGI may change another income-tested benefit, so the actual incremental tax change can be more complex than multiplying a contribution by a bracket percentage. It cannot be assumed that every pre-tax contribution returns the same cash-tax savings, particularly when credits and phaseouts are present.
worked: Total income $92,000; eligible Schedule 1 adjustments $2,000.
2026 standard deduction for a single non-elderly filer: $16,100.
In an otherwise eligible simple return, taxable income = $90,000 − $16,100 = $73,900.
practice: Why must a 401(k) deferral not be deducted again when Box 1 already excludes it?
It would recognize one economic reduction twice, artificially understating taxable income. Reconcile the wages and retirement contribution reporting first.
A student knows gross income but not AGI. What is missing?
The legal status and amount of allowable adjustments to income; gross receipts or gross pay alone do not establish the AGI line.

sections.title: Deduction, credit, payment and refund are four different concepts
body: A deduction reduces taxable income. A credit generally reduces the computed tax subject to specific rules. A nonrefundable credit cannot by itself create a tax refund beyond the liability it offsets; a refundable credit can in certain cases create or increase a refund. A payroll withholding payment is not a credit earned by the taxpayer for behavior: it is money already remitted to the government on the taxpayer's behalf. The difference matters because 'getting a refund' does not mean the household paid less tax.

For a simple one-dollar deduction at a 22% federal marginal rate, the first-order reduction in federal ordinary income tax is about $0.22. For an allowable $1,000 credit, the direct liability offset can be $1,000, subject to limits and phaseouts. The deduction can have additional interactions, and tax tables, special capital-gain rates or credits can make an exact return differ; the model must state those features explicitly.

The refund equation is total federal payments and allowable refundable credits minus total federal tax. If positive, a refund is due; if negative, the balance is an amount owed. Withholding changes settlement but not the underlying gross income or the tax computation. Optimizing only for the largest refund can mask lost liquidity during the year.
worked: Ordinary taxable income $70,000, approximate marginal rate 22%; eligible $1,000 deduction can save ~$220 before secondary effects.
Eligible $1,000 nonrefundable credit can directly reduce positive tax up to applicable limitations.
Tax after credits $8,000; withholding $9,250 ⇒ $1,250 refund.
Same tax $8,000; withholding $6,750 ⇒ $1,250 due; the underlying tax is identical.
practice: A friend says a tax deduction refunds its full cost. Explain the error.
A deduction subtracts from the tax base, not from tax dollar for dollar. Its tax effect depends on marginal rates and other constraints.
Does a $4,000 refund prove an efficient filing strategy?
No. It may largely represent excess withholding during the year; review actual total tax, credits, penalties, and cash-flow preferences.

sections.title: Complete 2026 single-filer example with qualified dividends
body: Consider a hypothetical US single filer who is under 65, has no dependents, takes the 2026 standard deduction, and has $85,000 W-2 Box 1 wages, $1,000 taxable interest, $1,500 qualified dividends included within $1,500 ordinary dividends, and $4,000 net long-term gain. There are no Schedule 1 adjustments, capital-loss carryovers, additional taxes or credits. We separate this deliberately simple case from a real Form 1040: special worksheets and the official tax tables can introduce rounding differences.

Total income and AGI are $91,500. Subtract the 2026 single-filer standard deduction of $16,100 to obtain $75,400 taxable income. Of this, $5,500 consists of eligible preferential-rate income, leaving $69,900 taxed at ordinary marginal brackets. The ordinary segment produces $1,240 on the first $12,400, $4,560 on the next $38,000, and $4,290 on the next $19,500 at 22%, totaling $10,090.

In 2026 the single-filer zero-rate capital-gain threshold is $49,450 of taxable income, and the 15% limit reaches $545,500. Because ordinary taxable income already exceeds $49,450, this example places the $5,500 preferred amount in the 15% band: $825. Approximate regular federal tax is therefore $10,915. If withholding is $13,000 and there are no additional taxes, credits or payments, the illustrated refund is $2,085. This ignores tax-table rounding and does not claim to be a filed return.
worked: Taxable = $91,500 − $16,100 = $75,400; preferred portion $5,500, ordinary portion $69,900.
practice: Where does the 2026 $49,450 capital-gain threshold enter this example?
The preferential income is stacked on top of ordinary taxable income. Because $69,900 already exceeds $49,450, none of the $5,500 qualifies for the zero-rate slice.
Which missing feature most directly prevents calling this a complete actual return?
Eligibility for credits and additional taxes, complete forms, any carryovers, special rate worksheets, official tax tables and factual documents all must be checked.

sections.title: From teaching model to defensible filed return
body: An academic model is a traceable approximation until it includes every applicable schedule and tax-year instruction. An actual return may require Form 8949 and Schedule D netting, Schedule C and self-employment tax, Schedule 2 additional taxes, Schedule 3 credits and payments, special deductions, phaseouts, capital-gain worksheets, estimated tax, Medicare-related taxes, and state returns. Tax rules can change between a year worked and a return filed in the next calendar year.

Source hierarchy matters. The current year's official forms and instructions answer how to submit, IRS publications explain common concepts, and state revenue agencies govern state adjustments. Recheck final 2026 filing forms when released for 2027 filing. An education app should label every rate by tax year, hold an effective date and verification URL, and never silently reuse one year's threshold in the next. Deductions and bracket amounts from 2025 must not be mixed with 2026 calculations.

Ethically, an adviser must not invent deductions, omit side-gig earnings, disguise taxable proceeds as transfers, or promise that ownership in a trust automatically eliminates tax. These cases can require an enrolled agent, CPA or tax attorney. An analyst's role is to identify the evidence, calculate alternative lawful outcomes, and explain uncertainty—not to guarantee a result.
worked: Prepare an audit trail: document → return line → adjustment → computation → withholding/payment.
Check applicable tax year, filing status, age, dependent status, residency and specialized schedules.
Recompute independently, compare to authoritative instructions and record any difference.
Keep personal details out of the educational lab; no account connections or tax preparation are implied.
practice: What does it mean for a tax model to be reproducible?
Another reviewer can trace every input to a dated source, follow the formula and assumptions, and obtain the same results within declared rounding rules.
Why must a 2026 tax model be updated before returns are filed in 2027?
The IRS may finalize forms and instructions or issue additional guidance; the curriculum should verify applicable year-specific law rather than treating preliminary education as filing advice.

assessment.title: Tax return reconstruction and source-control memo
assessment.prompt: An unmarried hypothetical 2026 filer age 35 has W-2 Box 1 wages $85,000; W-2 Box 2 withholding $13,000; taxable interest $1,000; ordinary dividends $1,500 of which $1,500 are qualified; and a verified long-term capital gain $4,000. Assume no other income, adjustments, credits, additional taxes or carryovers, and the standard deduction. Prepare total income, AGI, taxable income, ordinary-rate tax, special-rate tax, total federal income tax and refund. Then write 400–600 words explaining source-document verification, tax-year changes and three reasons a real return may differ.
rubric: 2026 bracket arithmetic and preferred-income stacking: 30 points
Professional limitations, ethical reasoning and sources: 20 points
answerKey: Qualified dividend and net long-term gain $5,500 stacked above $69,900 ordinary taxable income.
Ordinary $10,090; special-rate $825; approximate federal income tax $10,915.
Withholding $13,000 produces approximate $2,085 refund, ignoring official table rounding and omitted items.
Strong memo distinguishes 2026 law from final return forms, documents basis and qualified-dividend treatment, and states assumptions.
